evidence: Plin. NH 2.89: comētās Graecī vocant, nostrī crīnītās
terms.comment: The Greek word, taken into Latin; Seneca’s seventh book of Natural Questions is about comets. Accusative comētēn or comētam.
The Latin name Pliny gives beside the Greek: a comet is a star with hair, and its tail is its crīnis or coma.

phrases.latin: Ecce comētēs! Vidē quam longum crīnem trahat.
phrases.english: Look, a comet! See what a long tail it has.

phrases.latin: in ipsō caelō stēllae repente nāscuntur. … comētās Graecī vocant, nostrī crīnītās, horrentēs crīne sanguineō et comārum modō in vertice hispidās
phrases.english: in the sky itself stars are suddenly born. … The Greeks call them comets and we call them long-haired stars, bristling with blood-red hair and shaggy at the top like a head of hair

sources: Lewis & Short: cometes · Lewis & Short: crinitus
